description: Kiran Thapa Magar appointed Bagmati chief minister  The Himalayan Times
publisher.title: The Himalayan Times
full_article:
HETAUDA, AUGUST 21

Kiran Thapa Magar of the CPN-UML has been appointed chief minister of Bagmati Province, taking charge at the head of a coalition involving the NCP, UML and Rastriya Prajatantra Party.

Related Articles Kiran Thapa to take oath as Bagmati chief minister today RPP central leadership rejects support for UML's Kiran Thapa in Bagmati

Thapa Magar took the oath of office and secrecy before Bagmati Province Chief Deepak Prasad Devkota on Thursday.

The new chief minister has also formed part of his Cabinet, with Saral Sahyatri Poudel of the NCP appointed Minister for Economic Affairs and Planning; Raju Bista of the RPP Minister for Water Supply, Energy and Irrigation; Rajendra Prajapati Minister for Industry, Tourism, Labour and Transport; and Girbhadur Tamang Minister for Health and Social Development.

From the UML, Bharat KC has been appointed Minister for Physical Infrastructure, while Gyan Bahadur Tamang has been given the portfolio of minister without portfolio.

The 104-member Bagmati Provincial Assembly requires 53 lawmakers to form a majority. The NCP has 26 lawmakers, the UML 25 and the RPP 12, giving the three parties a combined strength of 63.

The new government was formed after former Chief Minister Indra Bahadur Baniya resigned on August 17. The province chief had set Thursday at 4pm as the deadline for parties to stake a claim to form a new government.

The NCP, UML and RPP had jointly staked their claim under Thapa Magar's leadership on Wednesday.

The UML had withdrawn its support for the previous government on August 6 and moved to form a new government.

Photo: Prakash Dahal

The provincial assembly has 36 Nepali Congress lawmakers, 26 from the NCP, 25 from the UML, 12 from the RPP, three from the Nepal Workers and Peasants Party and two from the Hamro Nepali Party.

Who is Kiran Thapa Magar?

Born on August 30, 1976 (B.S. 2033 Bhadra 14) in Suryabinayak Municipality-8 of Bhaktapur, Thapa Magar entered politics and social service in 2047 BS and has remained active in the field since then.

He has completed education up to the Intermediate level and currently serves as vice-chair of the UML Bhaktapur District Committee.

Thapa Magar was elected ward chair of Suryabinayak Municipality-8 in 2017 and also served as coordinator of the municipality's Social Development Committee.

He was elected to the Bagmati Provincial Assembly from Bhaktapur-2 (1) in 2022.

Before becoming chief minister, he served twice as Bagmati's health minister, from July 24, 2024 to June 2026, according to the information provided.

His political career has taken him from local government leadership to the provincial assembly and ministerial office, culminating in his appointment as chief minister.

KATHMANDU: Nepal will take on hosts NT Strike in their opening match of the ongoing Top End T20 cricket tournament in Australia today. The match is scheduled to begin at 2:15 pm Nepali time.

The Cricket Association of Nepal (CAN) has sent a 15-member Nepal ‘A’ squad to Australia under the captaincy of Anil Shah. The squad includes Kushal Bhurtel, Lokesh Bam, Tritaraj Das, Mayan Yadav, Pawan Sarraf, Deepak Dumre, Kushal Malla, Rashid Khan, Narayan Joshi, Akash Chand, Shahab Alam, Bipin Khatri, Yuvraj Khatri and Rijan Dhakal.

According to the tournament schedule, Nepal will play six matches in the league stage. Following today’s opening game against NT Strike, Nepal will face the Bangladesh ‘High-Performance’ team on August 22.

Nepal will then play the Hurricanes on August 24, the ACT Comets on August 26, the Kingsmen in its fifth match and Victoria in its final league match.

Nepal previously participated in the tournament’s last edition, winning two of its six matches and losing the remaining four.

title: Nepal Faces Recurring LPG Gas Shortages Due to Supply Issues and Consumer Hoarding - Ratopati
description: Nepal Faces Recurring LPG Gas Shortages Due to Supply Issues and Consumer Hoarding  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. Be it the festive season or the onset of winter, election hustle or international war alarms, the first fear in Nepali society starts from the kitchen – 'Will we not get gas anymore!'

Analyzing the data and trends of the last decade (from 2072 to 2083 BS), it is seen that Nepali consumers have faced extreme hardship and shortage of gas at least five times.

It has been found that about 90 percent of the gas shortage in Nepal is not due to a complete halt in actual supply, but rather related to international circumstances, blockade or war fears, and subsequent unnecessary hoarding by consumers, along with weak government management.

The gas shortage that started in the last period from Magh-Falgun 2082 BS has not eased even by Bhadra 2083 BS. Mansir-Poush is considered a month of high gas consumption due to winter. It was during this time that gas imports were affected after problems arose in Indian refineries. Consumers were not getting gas due to insufficient gas imports to meet market demand. Due to the fear of supply system disruption caused by the Israel-Iran conflict in West Asia, Nepal Oil Corporation adopted a policy of providing only 7.1 kg per cylinder as a precaution in Falgun 2082 BS.

Although the distribution of full cylinders (14.2 kg) was resumed from Asar 31, 2083 BS after about four months, the market did not normalize. As millions of empty cylinders from consumers who had been using half cylinders for a long time came to the market at once for refilling, a situation of inability to meet demand (backlog) was created. Although more than 100 bullets are being imported daily from India, due to the chaos in the distribution system and consumers hoarding more than necessary, the corporation itself had to distribute gas from depots.

Series of Gas Shortages

The history of LPG gas for cooking in Nepal is more than five and a half decades old. In the era of firewood and kerosene in the fiscal year 2022/023 BS, gas imports from India first started in October 2026 BS. In the initial days, it was brought directly filled in cylinders from India and was limited to the kitchens of the royal family and the influential.

As dependence on foreign fuel increased, the first gas bottling plant in the country was established in 2028 BS in the name of Nepal Gas. After that, gas started being brought in bullets from India and filled in Nepal. Today, 58 gas industries are in operation in the country, and gas has fallen from a symbol of prosperity to a basic necessity for citizens, but its supply is always in crisis, even though access is easy.

According to Shivaprasad Ghimire, former president of the Nepal LP Gas Industry Association, gas was not accessible to ordinary citizens in the early days. 'At that time, cooking with gas was like a class identity for the royal family and the Rana family; firewood and kerosene were the alternatives for the general public,' Ghimire recalled.

Gas distribution, which started commercially 52 years ago, has become a mandatory necessity for every household today. According to Ghimire, Nepal has faced three major historical gas crises — the blockade of 2045 BS, the earthquake and blockade of 2072 BS, and the COVID-19 pandemic.

A few months after the devastating earthquake of 2072 BS, Nepal experienced the biggest fuel crisis in its history due to the 'Madhesh Movement and India's undeclared blockade'. With bullets stopped at the border for about 6 months from Ashwin to Falgun, the general public was forced to queue for weeks. During the same period, the government started the practice of distributing half cylinders of gas for the first time.

In 2074 BS, due to floods in the Terai obstructing roads and the movement of gas industrialists and transport entrepreneurs demanding an increase in commission in Falgun, there was a partial gas shortage in the market for 1 to 2 weeks. The supply was imbalanced due to consumers hoarding cylinders in fear of price hikes.

As COVID-19 spread worldwide, a 'lockdown rumor and fear' spread in Nepal from the end of Phagun to Chaitra 2076 BS. Although the supply at the border was not stopped, due to the fear of a crisis similar to a blockade, consumers hoarded more cylinders than necessary, leading to an artificial shortage in the market for a few weeks.

In 2081 BS, the general public faced a gas shortage for about a month and a half after the Nepal LP Gas Industry Association stopped selling gas demanding an increase in commission and transportation fares. The supply only normalized after an agreement was reached between the government and the traders to increase the commission on Falgun 20 BS.

When did Nepal face LPG gas shortages?

Over 4 Million Gas Cylinders Consumed in Shrawan Alone

According to the corporation, 4,036,364 cylinders of gas were sold and consumed in the month of Shrawan alone. This is the highest so far, the corporation stated. This quantity is also about 9 lakh cylinders more than the previous month, Asar. In Asar, 3,136,937 cylinders were sold.

Consumption per Month?

Chaitra 2082: 2,732,355 cylinders

Baishakh 2083: 2,257,496 cylinders

Jeth 2083: 2,312,837 cylinders

Asar 2083: 3,136,937 cylinders

Shrawan 2083: 4,036,364 cylinders

Despite the excessive distribution of gas in Shrawan, the public's complaint of not getting gas has not disappeared.

Gas Imports Increasing

According to the data published by Nepal Oil Corporation, there is data on gas imports and consumption only from the fiscal year 2050/051 BS onwards. The quantity imported before that is not mentioned. The corporation stated that 9,308 metric tons of gas were imported and sold in the fiscal year 2050/051 BS. Similarly, 13,049 metric tons were imported and sold in 2051/052 BS. While 9,308 metric tons of gas were imported annually three decades ago, the data shows that consumption is now over 500,000 metric tons annually. Not only this, but the data shows that the use of cooking gas is increasing every year.

It is mentioned that 521,529 metric tons were imported in the fiscal year 2082/083 BS. The import quantity in the fiscal year 2082/083 BS is about 56 times more than in the fiscal year 2050/051 BS.

How much gas was imported each year?

The import and consumption of LPG gas for cooking in Nepal have more than doubled in the last decade. While the data from fiscal year 2072/073 BS to 2082/083 BS shows a sharp overall increase in gas imports, there have been some fluctuations in recent years.

Ten years ago, in the fiscal year 2072/073 BS, the volume of gas imports in Nepal was only 214,194 metric tons. In a decade, this volume has increased significantly, reaching an all-time high of 555,111 metric tons in the fiscal year 2081/082 BS. This volume is more than two and a half times the initial year.

In the fiscal year 2082/083 BS, gas imports decreased slightly to 521,529 metric tons. According to the data, gas imports were continuously increasing from fiscal year 2072/073 BS to 2078/079 BS. In the fiscal year 2078/079 BS, gas imports reached 536,028 metric tons, but in the fiscal year 2079/080 BS, it decreased for the first time to 512,000 metric tons.

Main Reason for Shortage is Lack of Storage and Psychological Fear

Stakeholders say that the recurring shortage of LPG gas for cooking in Nepal is due to 'psychological fear' spreading among consumers, lack of storage capacity, and weak electrical infrastructure.

The Ministry of Industry, Commerce and Supplies stated that the supply of LPG gas for cooking is normal in the market, and gas shortages occur due to unnecessary hoarding by consumers out of fear of future unavailability. The ministry also acknowledged that the lack of adequate gas storage capacity is a problem.

Similarly, Diwan Bahadur Chand, president of the Nepal LP Gas Industry Association, says that the main reason for the gas shortage in the market is the psychological fear seen in both consumers and sellers. He said, 'The problem has arisen because consumers, fearing they won't get gas, try to stock filled cylinders rather than exchanging empty ones. The number of people waiting for stock to arrive is higher than those looking to buy new gas.'

Likewise, former president of the association, Shivaprasad Ghimire, stated that the current shortage is not due to a decrease in imports but due to consumers, remembering past hardships, trying to stock 5 to 10 cylinders at home. He argues that even though there are 59 gas industries in the country, the market gets disrupted by minor disturbances due to the lack of 90 days of strategic storage (buffer stock). Ghimire said, 'The market appears to be in shortage because consumers, remembering past hardships, try to stock 5-10 cylinders to last for 2 months. If consumers do not hoard gas unnecessarily, the market will normalize.' He argued for reducing the number of brands, stating that the large number of gas brands in Nepal creates significant problems in cylinder management.

Binita Mani Upadhyay, Director of the LPG and Aviation Department at Nepal Oil Corporation, said that Nepal has a reverse policy of selling electricity worth 12 billion rupees at a profit and buying foreign gas worth 55 to 60 billion rupees. He stated that even though electricity has reached 96 percent of households in the country, citizens cannot switch to induction stoves due to unreliable infrastructure.

'People have not been able to give up gas due to transformer capacity issues, voltage fluctuations, and frequent power outages. It is difficult to reduce dependence on gas unless the government makes policies for infrastructure development. Consumers also hoard unnecessary gas when the media publishes sensitive headlines and rumors spread,' he said.

Electricity as a Long-Term Alternative to Gas

Ganesh Karki, former president of the Independent Power Producers' Association, Nepal (IPPAN) and energy expert, emphasized that electricity should be made an alternative to gas for cooking to ensure energy security and end dependence in Nepal.

In a conversation with Ratopati, Karki pointed out the need to significantly increase domestic consumption of electricity as Nepal is currently producing sufficient electricity. He stated that with the end of load shedding in the country, priority should be given to the use of electricity for cooking, operating induction stoves, and for domestic and industrial purposes.

'The kitchen of Nepalis is always at risk of being affected by minor disruptions or fluctuations in the international petroleum market,' Karki said, 'Therefore, we must displace gas by increasing domestic production to last throughout the year, and its main alternative is electricity.'

He stated that the government should focus on policy clarity and infrastructure development to encourage the use of electrical energy. He believes that increasing domestic consumption of electricity produced in Nepal will reduce dependence and automatically solve many problems in the energy sector. Karki emphasized the need for the government to provide concessions and facilities to encourage users of induction stoves and other electrical appliances, and urged the general public to be aware of using domestic electricity. He claimed that increased electricity consumption contributes to the country's economic prosperity and frees it from dependence on imported fuel.

Ghimire, however, argued that it is not immediately possible to replace gas with electricity, even though the government has a policy to promote electricity use, due to weak infrastructure. He said, 'Even though the government has a policy to displace gas by using induction now, it is impossible to replace gas until the capacity of household wiring, transformers, and transmission lines is improved. The state should prioritize the construction of gas pipelines. Also, in the long term, the PPP model should be adopted to increase storage capacity.' He mentioned that building pipelines would save transportation costs.

As a second measure, he proposed the merger of gas industries. He suggested reducing the 59 industries to a limited number of brands. Similarly, he stated that to manage the subsidy given on gas, a system of 'cashback' (cash subsidy) directly to the bank accounts of the target group should be implemented in Nepal, similar to India.

What is the government doing for a long-term solution?

Netra Prasad Subedi, Joint Secretary and Spokesperson of the Ministry of Industry, Commerce and Supplies, said that the government is serious about solving the gas problem in the country. He informed that the government is discussing future plans regarding gas import and alternative arrangements.

'Nepal does not produce gas currently. Even if some is produced in the future, we have realized the need to increase gas storage to manage emergency situations for now,' said Spokesperson Subedi. 'We are discussing increasing storage capacity to last for at least one to two months for emergency situations.'

According to Spokesperson Subedi, to prevent problems like the current one in the future, Nepal Oil Corporation is preparing to monitor the stock and movement of gas cylinders by implementing GIS mapping and QR systems. Additionally, Nepal Oil Corporation has already studied the Motihari-Sarlahi pipeline project for gas import. Although a proposal has been put forward for the construction of the project, the final 'go-ahead' (approval) from the ministry is still pending. The ministry stated that the distribution system will be further improved by constructing storage facilities after the pipeline is expanded.

Furthermore, regarding the exploration of petroleum products (gas) in Dailekh, the Chinese side has completed the first phase of testing and submitted the report. Spokesperson Subedi said that the Nepali government wishes for the Chinese government to take responsibility for the next phase of work, but a further response from the Chinese side is awaited.

The ministry is also making efforts to encourage consumers to use electrical appliances like induction stoves as an alternative to LPG gas, considering that electricity is energy produced within Nepal and a lot of electricity goes to waste in the summer. This issue has also been raised in parliamentary committees, and Spokesperson Subedi stated that it should be brought as a package in collaboration with the Ministry of Energy. Although the import of induction stoves has increased recently, there is a need to introduce further concessions and promotional programs.

कमी कें मुख्य कारण भंडारण कें कमी आ मनोवैज्ञानिक भय छै

नेपाल मे खाना बनाबय लेल एलपीजी गैस के बार-बार कमी के कारण उपभोक्ता मे पसरल ‘मनोवैज्ञानिक भय’, भंडारण क्षमता के कमी, आ कमजोर विद्युत बुनियादी ढांचा के कारण सरोकारवाला के कहनाय छनि.

उद्योग, वाणिज्य आरू आपूर्ति मंत्रालय न॑ कहलकै कि खाना बनाबै लेली एलपीजी गैस के आपूर्ति बाजार म॑ सामान्य छै, आरू भविष्य म॑ अनुपलब्धता के डर स॑ उपभोक्ता द्वारा अनावश्यक जमाखोरी के कारण गैस के कमी होय छै । मंत्रालय इहो स्वीकार केलक अछि जे पर्याप्त गैस भंडारण क्षमता के कमी एकटा समस्या अछि.

तहिना नेपाल एलपी गैस उद्योग संघक अध्यक्ष दीवान बहादुर चन्द बजारमे गैसक कमीक मुख्य कारण उपभोक्ता आ विक्रेता दुनूमे देखल मनोवैज्ञानिक भय बतौलनि । ओ कहलनि जे, समस्या एहि लेल उठल अछि जे उपभोक्ता गैस नहि भेटबाक डर सं खाली सिलेंडर के आदान-प्रदान करय सं बेसी भरल सिलेंडर के स्टॉक करय के कोशिश करैत छथिन्ह. स्टॉक आबय के इंतजार करय वाला लोक के संख्या नव गैस खरीदय चाहय वाला लोक सं बेसि अछि.'

तहिना एसोसिएशन के पूर्व अध्यक्ष शिवप्रसाद घिमिरे के कहनाय छनि जे वर्तमान कमी आयात मे कमी के कारण नहिं बल्कि उपभोक्ता के कारण अछि, पिछला कठिनाई के याद करैत, घर मे 5 सं 10 सिलेंडर के स्टॉक करय के कोशिश. हुनकऽ तर्क छै कि देश म॑ ५९ गैस उद्योग होय के बावजूद ९० दिन के रणनीतिक भंडारण (बफर स्टॉक) के कमी के वजह स॑ बाजार म॑ छोटऽ-मोट गड़बड़ी होय जाय छै । घिमिरे कहलनि जे, बाजार मे कमी देखा रहल अछि, किया कि उपभोक्ता पिछला कठिनाई कए याद करैत 5-10 सिलेंडर कए 2 महीना तक चलबाक लेल स्टॉक करबाक कोशिश करैत छथि। अगर उपभोक्ता अनावश्यक रूप स गैस क जमाखोरी नहि करत त बाजार सामान्य भ जाएत।' नेपाल मे गैस ब्रांड क पैघ संख्या स सिलेंडर प्रबंधन मे काफी समस्या पैदा होइत अछि इति कहैत ओ ब्रांड क संख्या कम करबाक तर्क देलथि।

नेपाल तेल निगमके एलपीजी आ विमानन विभागके निदेशक बिनिता मणि उपाध्याय नेपालमे १२ अरब रुपैयाँके बिजली मुनाफामे बेचके ५५ सँ ६० अरब रुपैयाके विदेशी गैस खरीदैके उल्टा नीति रहल बटैलै । ओ कहलनि जे, देश मे 96 प्रतिशत घर मे बिजली पहुंच गेलाक बादो अविश्वसनीय बुनियादी ढांचा के कारण नागरिक इंडक्शन स्टोव पर नहि आबि सकैत छथि।

'ट्रांसफार्मर के क्षमता के मुद्दा, वोल्टेज में उतार-चढ़ाव, आ बेर-बेर बिजली बंद होय के कारण लोक गैस नै छोड़ि सकल अछि।' जा धरि सरकार बुनियादी ढांचा विकास लेल नीति नहि बनाओत ता धरि गैस पर निर्भरता कम करब मुश्किल अछि। उपभोक्ता जखन मीडिया संवेदनशील हेडलाइन प्रकाशित करैत अछि आ अफवाह फैलैत अछि तखन अनावश्यक गैस सेहो जमा करैत अछि।'

इहो पढ़ू गैस संकट के स्थायी समाधान : 59 ब्रांड के विलय, पाइपलाइन आओर लक्षित सब्सिडी

गैस के दीर्घकालिक विकल्प के रूप मे बिजली

नेपालक स्वतन्त्र विद्युत उत्पादक संघ नेपालक पूर्व अध्यक्ष आ ऊर्जा विशेषज्ञ गणेश कार्की नेपालमे ऊर्जा सुरक्षा सुनिश्चित आ निर्भरता समाप्त करबाक लेल खाना बनाबय लेल गैस के विकल्प बनाबय पर जोर देलनि ।

राटोपति सं बातचीत मे कार्की नेपाल मे एखन पर्याप्त बिजली उत्पादन भ रहल अछि ताहि लेल घरेलु बिजली खपत मे काफी वृद्धि करबाक आवश्यकता बतौलनि। हुनकऽ कहना छै कि देश म॑ लोड शेडिंग के अंत के साथ खाना बनाबै, इंडक्शन स्टोव चलाबै, आरू घरेलू आरू औद्योगिक उद्देश्य लेली बिजली के उपयोग क॑ प्राथमिकता देलऽ जाय ।

कार्की कहलनि जे, ‘अन्तर्राष्ट्रीय पेट्रोलियम बाजार मे छोट-मोट व्यवधान या उतार-चढ़ाव स नेपाली के भनसा घर हमेशा प्रभावित होय के खतरा रहैत अछि, ताहि लेल हमरा सब के साल भरि चलय लेल घरेलू उत्पादन बढ़ा क गैस के विस्थापित करय पड़त, आ एकर मुख्य विकल्प बिजली अछि।’

Also Read 'अरबों रुपया के गैस आयात क घाटा करय के बजाय देश के भीतर बिजली के खपत बढ़ाबय के चाही'.

हुनी कहलकै कि सरकार क नीति स्पष्टता आरू बुनियादी ढांचा विकास प ध्यान देना चाहिय्यौ ताकि विद्युत ऊर्जा के उपयोग क प्रोत्साहित करलौ जाय सकै । हुनकऽ मानना ​​छै कि नेपाल म॑ उत्पादित बिजली केरऽ घरेलू खपत बढ़ला स॑ निर्भरता कम होय जैतै आरू ऊर्जा क्षेत्र केरऽ बहुत समस्या के स्वतः समाधान होय ​​जैतै । कार्की न॑ सरकार क॑ इंडक्शन स्टोव आरू अन्य विद्युत उपकरणऽ के उपयोग करै वाला क॑ प्रोत्साहित करै लेली रियायत आरू सुविधा उपलब्ध करै के जरूरत प॑ जोर देलकै, आरू आम जनता स॑ घरेलू बिजली के उपयोग के प्रति जागरूक रहै के आग्रह करलकै । हुनकऽ दावा छेलै कि बिजली के खपत बढ़ला स॑ देश केरऽ आर्थिक समृद्धि म॑ योगदान होय ​​छै आरू आयातित ईंधन प॑ निर्भरता स॑ मुक्त होय जाय छै ।

लेकिन घिमिरे के तर्क छेलै कि कमजोर बुनियादी ढाँचा के वजह स॑ सरकार के पास बिजली के उपयोग क॑ बढ़ावा दै के नीति रहला के बावजूद गैस के जगह बिजली स॑ बदलना तत्काल संभव नै छै । हुनी कहलकै, 'भले ही सरकार के पास अब॑ इंडक्शन के इस्तेमाल करी क॑ गैस क॑ विस्थापित करै के नीति छै, लेकिन जब॑ तलक घरऽ के तार, ट्रांसफार्मर, आरू ट्रांसमिशन लाइन के क्षमता म॑ सुधार नै होय जाय छै, गैस बदलना असंभव छै । राज्य कए गैस पाइपलाइन क निर्माण कए प्राथमिकता देबाक चाही। संगहि दीर्घकाल मे भंडारण क्षमता बढ़ेबा लेल पीपीपी मॉडल अपनाउल जेबाक चाही।' ओ पाइपलाइन बनेबा स परिवहन क खर्च मे बचत हेबाक जिक्र केलथि।

दोसर उपाय क रूप मे ओ गैस उद्योग क विलय क प्रस्ताव रखलथि। ओ 59 उद्योग कए सीमित संख्या मे ब्रांड बनेबाक सुझाव देलथि। तहिना ओ कहलनि जे, गैस पर देल गेल सब्सिडी के प्रबंधन के लेल भारत के समान नेपाल मे सीधा लक्षित समूह के बैंक खाता मे ‘कैशबैक’ (कैश सब्सिडी) के व्यवस्था लागू करबाक चाही।

दीर्घकालीन समाधान के लेल सरकार की क रहल अछि?

उद्योग, वाणिज्य आ आपूर्ति मन्त्रालयके संयुक्त सचिव आ प्रवक्ता नेत्रप्रसाद सुबेदी देशमे गैस समस्याके समाधानके लेल सरकार गम्भीर रहल बतौलनि । ओ जानकारी देलनि जे सरकार गैस आयात आ वैकल्पिक व्यवस्था क संबंध मे भविष्य क योजना पर चर्चा क रहल अछि।

'नेपालमे एखन गैसक उत्पादन नहि होइत अछि ।' भले ही भविष्य म॑ कुछ उत्पादन होय ​​जाय, लेकिन फिलहाल आपातकालीन स्थिति के प्रबंधन लेली गैस के भंडारण बढ़ाबै के जरूरत के अहसास होय गेलऽ छै,’ प्रवक्ता सुबेदी न॑ कहलकै । 'हम आपातकालीन स्थिति के लेल कम सं कम एक सं दू महीना तक चलय लेल भंडारण क्षमता बढ़ाबय पर चर्चा क रहल छी.'

प्रवक्ता सुबेदी के अनुसार भविष्य मे वर्तमान समस्या जेकाँ समस्या के रोकथाम के लेल नेपाल तेल निगम जीआईएस मैपिंग आ क्यूआर सिस्टम लागू क गैस सिलेंडर के भंडार आ आवाजाही के निगरानी के तैयारी क रहल अछि। एकर अतिरिक्त नेपाल तेल निगम गैस आयात के लेल मोतिहारी-सरलाही पाइपलाइन परियोजना के अध्ययन क चुकल अछि। हालांकि एहि परियोजना क निर्माण क लेल प्रस्ताव राखल गेल अछि, मुदा मंत्रालय स अंतिम ‘गो-एहेड’ (अनुमोदन) एखन धरि लंबित अछि। मंत्रालय के कहनाय छनि जे पाइप लाइन के विस्तार के बाद भंडारण सुविधा के निर्माण क वितरण प्रणाली मे आओर सुधार कएल जाएत.

एकरऽ अलावा दैलेख म॑ पेट्रोलियम उत्पाद (गैस) के खोज के संबंध म॑ चीनी पक्ष न॑ पहलऽ चरण के परीक्षण पूरा करी क॑ रिपोर्ट जमा करी देल॑ छै । प्रवक्ता सुबेदी कहलनि जे, नेपाली सरकार के इच्छा अछि जे चीन सरकार अगिला चरण के काज के जिम्मेदारी लेत, मुदा चीनी पक्ष के आगू के प्रतिक्रिया के इंतजार अछि।

मंत्रालय नेपाल के भीतर बिजली उत्पादित ऊर्जा छै आरू गर्मी में बहुत बिजली बेकार होय जाय छै, ई बात क देखत॑ हुअ॑ उपभोक्ता सिनी क॑ एलपीजी गैस के विकल्प के रूप म॑ इंडक्शन स्टोव जैसनऽ विद्युत उपकरण के उपयोग करै लेली भी प्रोत्साहित करै के प्रयास करी रहलऽ छै । ई मुद्दा संसदीय समिति म॑ भी उठलऽ छै, आरू प्रवक्ता सुबेदी न॑ कहलकै कि एकरा ऊर्जा मंत्रालय के सहयोग स॑ पैकेज के रूप म॑ लानलऽ जाय । हालांकि हाल मे इंडक्शन स्टोव के आयात बढ़ल अछि मुदा आओर रियायत आओर प्रचार कार्यक्रम शुरू करय के जरूरत अछि.

full_article:
Nepal has emerged from several turbulent years with a more stable economy, stronger financial buffers and improved economic institutions, even as earthquakes, floods, political changes and global pressures repeatedly disrupted its recovery. The country recently completed its first IMF-supported arrangement in nearly two decades, marking an important milestone after a reform programme that began in 2022.

Nepal Mission Chief Sarwat Jahan said the biggest achievement is not simply that major economic indicators have improved, but that reforms continued through an unusually difficult period. A consistent policy direction, adjustments to changing political conditions and technical support helped the country keep the programme on course.

Inflation Falls as Nepal Rebuilds Its Financial Buffers

The improvement can be seen clearly in inflation, foreign exchange reserves and government finances. Average inflation, which stood at 7.7% in fiscal year 2022–23, dropped to 1.7% in the first half of fiscal year 2025–26, easing pressure on household purchasing power. International reserves also strengthened from around nine months of import cover to more than twelve months, giving Nepal greater protection against currency pressures, expensive imports and disruptions in external trade.

Public finances became healthier as the budget gap narrowed substantially, while public debt remained at low risk of distress. These gains provide the government with more room to respond when economic emergencies or natural disasters require additional spending. Maintaining this progress was difficult because Nepal faced repeated setbacks.

A major earthquake struck in 2023, severe floods followed in 2024, and social unrest created further uncertainty. Higher energy prices associated with the war in the Middle East have added another source of pressure, while repeated disruptions have slowed the recovery and weighed on job creation. The experience has reinforced the importance of building economic resilience before a crisis arrives, particularly through stronger institutions and sufficient financial buffers that can soften the impact of unexpected shocks.

Institutional Reforms Could Have the Longest Impact

Nepal's reforms attracted less public attention because they focused on the institutions behind economic decision-making rather than immediate changes people could see. The country modernized the way its central bank conducts monetary policy and strengthened financial-sector oversight, including improvements to bank supervision and reviews of loan quality. Fiscal transparency increased through the publication of financial statements for state-owned enterprises, while authorities developed a revenue mobilization strategy and improved the planning and management of public investment.

Nepal upgraded its anti-money-laundering legislation and moved toward strengthening the central bank's legal framework and accountability. Together, these measures are intended to make economic policies more reliable and effective over time, reducing vulnerabilities that can become especially damaging when the country faces another major shock.

Stability Must Now Translate Into Jobs and Inclusive Growth

Nepal's next challenge is turning macroeconomic stability into improvements that people can experience through better jobs, higher incomes and stronger economic opportunities. Private investment remains too weak to generate the level of employment and growth the country needs. Vulnerabilities also remain within parts of the financial system, particularly among savings and credit cooperatives that provide financial services to large numbers of people.

Nepalese authorities have started an IMF Governance and Corruption Diagnostic to identify weaknesses, address governance gaps and help rebuild public trust. Completing the IMF-supported programme therefore represents a foundation rather than an endpoint. Continued priorities include strengthening the financial sector, improving social protection, attracting private investment and creating conditions in which economic growth can reach a broader share of the population.

Nepal has shown that reforms can continue even through political transitions, natural disasters and global economic shocks. Keeping that momentum could help the country create more employment, raise living standards and build greater protection against future crises, while the IMF has said it will continue supporting Nepal as the country moves from economic stabilisation toward stronger and more inclusive growth.

नेपाल कतेको उथल-पुथल वर्ष सँ बेसी स्थिर अर्थव्यवस्था, मजबूत वित्तीय बफर आ सुधारल आर्थिक संस्थाक संग उभरल अछि, एतय तक कि भूकम्प, बाढ़ि, राजनीतिक परिवर्तन आ वैश्विक दबाव बेर-बेर एकर पुनर्प्राप्ति मे बाधा उत्पन्न केलक । देश न॑ हाल ही म॑ लगभग दू दशक म॑ आईएमएफ द्वारा समर्थित अपनऽ पहलऽ व्यवस्था पूरा करलकै, जे २०२२ म॑ शुरू होलऽ सुधार कार्यक्रम के बाद एगो महत्वपूर्ण मील के पत्थर छेकै ।

नेपाल मिशन प्रमुख सरवतजहान कहलनि जे, सबसँ पैघ उपलब्धि मात्र ई नहि अछि जे प्रमुख आर्थिक सूचक मे सुधार भेल अछि, अपितु असामान्य रूप सँ कठिन काल मे सुधार जारी रहल। लगातार नीतिगत दिशा, बदलतऽ राजनीतिक परिस्थिति म॑ समायोजन आरू तकनीकी सहायता न॑ देश क॑ कार्यक्रम क॑ रास्ता प॑ रखै म॑ मदद करलकै ।

नेपाल अपन वित्तीय बफर के पुनर्निर्माण के संग महंगाई गिरैत अछि

महंगाई, विदेशी मुद्रा भंडार आ सरकारी वित्त मे सुधार साफ देखल जा सकैत अछि। औसत महंगाई, जे वित्तीय वर्ष 2022-23 म॑ 7.7% छेलै, वित्तीय वर्ष 2025-26 केरऽ पहिलऽ छमाही म॑ गिरी क॑ 1.7% होय गेलै, जेकरा स॑ घरेलू क्रय शक्ति प॑ दबाव कम होय गेलै । अंतरराष्ट्रीय भंडार सेहो करीब नौ मासक आयात कवर स मजबूत भ गेल आ बारह मास स बेसी भ गेल, जाहि स नेपाल कए मुद्रा क दबाव, महग आयात आ बाहरी व्यापार मे बाधा स बेसी सुरक्षा भेटल।

बजट अंतर काफी कम भेला स सार्वजनिक वित्त स्वस्थ भ गेल, जखन कि सार्वजनिक ऋण पर संकट क खतरा कम रहल। ई लाभ स॑ सरकार क॑ आर्थिक आपातकाल या प्राकृतिक आपदा म॑ अतिरिक्त खर्च के जरूरत पड़ला प॑ जवाब दै के अधिक गुंजाइश मिलै छै । एहि प्रगति के कायम राखब कठिन छल कारण नेपाल के बेर-बेर असफलता के सामना करय पड़ैत छल.

2023 में एकटा पैघ भूकंप आयल छल, 2024 में एकर बाद भयंकर बाढ़ि आयल छल, आ सामाजिक अशांति के कारण आओर अनिश्चितता पैदा भेल छल. मध्य पूर्व म॑ युद्ध स॑ जुड़लऽ ऊर्जा केरऽ दाम बढ़ला स॑ दबाव केरऽ एगो आरू स्रोत बढ़ी गेलऽ छै, जबकि बार-बार बाधा के वजह स॑ रिकवरी म॑ धीमापन आबी गेलऽ छै आरू रोजगार सृजन प॑ भारी पड़लऽ छै । अनुभव न॑ संकट केरऽ आबै स॑ पहल॑ आर्थिक लचीलापन बनाबै के महत्व क॑ मजबूत करी देल॑ छै, खास करी क॑ मजबूत संस्थान आरू पर्याप्त वित्तीय बफर के माध्यम स॑ जे अप्रत्याशित झटका के प्रभाव क॑ नरम करी सकै छै ।

संस्थागत सुधार केरऽ सबसें लम्बा प्रभाव पड़॑ सकै छै

नेपालक सुधार जनताक ध्यान कम आकर्षित केलक, कारण एहि मे तत्काल परिवर्तन लोक देखि सकैत छल ताहि सँ बेसी आर्थिक निर्णय लेबाक पाछूक संस्था पर केन्द्रित छल । देश न॑ अपनऽ केंद्रीय बैंक केरऽ मौद्रिक नीति के संचालन के तरीका क॑ आधुनिक बनाबै आरू वित्तीय-क्षेत्र केरऽ निगरानी क॑ मजबूत करलकै, जेकरा म॑ बैंकऽ के पर्यवेक्षण म॑ सुधार आरू ऋण के गुणवत्ता के समीक्षा शामिल छै । सरकारी उद्यमऽ लेली वित्तीय विवरण के प्रकाशन के माध्यम स॑ राजकोषीय पारदर्शिता बढ़ी गेलै, जबकि अधिकारियऽ न॑ राजस्व जुटान के रणनीति तैयार करलकै आरू सार्वजनिक निवेश के योजना आरू प्रबंधन म॑ सुधार करलकै ।

नेपाल अपन मनी लांड्रिंग विरोधी कानून कए उन्नयन कए केंद्रीय बैंक क कानूनी ढांचा आ जवाबदेही कए मजबूत करबाक दिशा मे आगू बढ़ल। ई उपाय सब मिल क॑ समय के साथ आर्थिक नीति क॑ अधिक विश्वसनीय आरू प्रभावी बनाबै के उद्देश्य छै, जेकरा स॑ कमजोरी क॑ कम करलऽ जाय जे विशेष रूप स॑ नुकसानदेह होय सकै छै जब॑ देश क॑ एगो आरू बड़ऽ झटका के सामना करना पड़ै छै ।

स्थिरता आब नौकरी आ समावेशी विकास मे बदलय पड़त

नेपाल के अगिला चुनौती अछि स्थूल आर्थिक स्थिरता के सुधार में बदलब जेकर अनुभव लोक बेहतर नौकरी, बेसी आय आ मजबूत आर्थिक अवसर के माध्यम सं क सकैत अछि. निजी निवेश बहुत कमजोर बनल अछि जे देश कए जरूरत क रोजगार आ विकास क स्तर पैदा नहि करि सकैत अछि। वित्तीय प्रणाली कें किच्छू हिस्साक कें भीतर सेहो कमजोरी बनल छै, खासकर बचत आ ऋण सहकारी संस्थाक कें बीच जे पैघ संख्या मे लोगक कें वित्तीय सेवाक प्रदान करयत छै.

नेपाली प्राधिकारी सब कमजोरी के पहचान करय, शासन के अंतराल के दूर करय आ जनविश्वास के पुनर्निर्माण में मदद करय लेल आईएमएफ के शासन आ भ्रष्टाचार निदान शुरू केलक अछि. अइ लेल आईएमएफ समर्थित कार्यक्रम पूरा करनाय एकटा अंतिम बिंदु कें बजाय एकटा नींव कें प्रतिनिधित्व करय छै. निरंतर प्राथमिकता मे वित्तीय क्षेत्र कें मजबूत करनाय, सामाजिक सुरक्षा मे सुधार करनाय, निजी निवेश कें आकर्षित करनाय आ ऐहन परिस्थितिक कें निर्माण करनाय शामिल छै, जइ मे आर्थिक विकास आबादी कें एकटा व्यापक हिस्सा तइक पहुंच सकय.

नेपाल राजनीतिक संक्रमण, प्राकृतिक आपदा आ वैश्विक आर्थिक झटका के माध्यम स सेहो सुधार जारी राखि सकैत अछि से देखौलक अछि । ओहि गति के कायम रखला स देश के बेसी रोजगार सृजन, जीवन स्तर बढ़ाबय आ भविष्य के संकट के खिलाफ बेसी सुरक्षा के निर्माण में मदद मिल सकैत अछि, जखन कि आईएमएफ के कहनाय छनि जे देश आर्थिक स्थिरता स मजबूत आ समावेशी विकास दिस बढ़ैत नेपाल के सहयोग जारी राखत।

title: Supreme Court annuls Nepal Airlines executive chairman Shrestha’s appointment - OnlineKhabar English News
description: Supreme Court annuls Nepal Airlines executive chairman Shrestha’s appointment  OnlineKhabar English News
publisher.title: OnlineKhabar English News
full_article:
Kathmandu, August 21

The Supreme Court has annulled the government’s appointment of Maheshwor Bhakta Shrestha as executive chairman of Nepal Airlines Corporation.

A bench of Justices Sunil Kumar Pokharel and Balkrishna Dhakal, conducting the final hearing on a writ petition filed by Upendra Bahadur Karki against Shrestha, ruled on Thursday that his appointment was not in accordance with the law. However, the court said Karki’s claim that he should be appointed chairman himself was not substantiated.

Shrestha’s appointment as executive chairman and general manager of the corporation was also found to have violated the government’s appointment procedures. Under the Standards on Appointment and Nomination of Members and Office-Bearers of Public Bodies, 2016, issued by the Ministry of Tourism, a person appointed as the executive head of a public body must be at least 30 years old and not more than 65 years old.

Karki had filed the writ petition arguing that Shrestha was over 65 years old and had been appointed 34 years after retiring from the corporation. With the Supreme Court’s ruling, Shrestha has been removed from the post, and the government will now have to appoint an executive chairman through a new process. He will, however, continue to serve as a member of the board of directors.

Shrestha was also among five board members whose appointments had previously been annulled by the Supreme Court. On May 14, five members were appointed to the corporation’s board of directors. The Supreme Court later annulled those appointments, with Shrestha among the five. The court had also annulled those appointments while hearing a writ petition filed by Karki.

title: Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal Advocates for Nepal as a 'Dynamic and Reliable Bridge' Between Two Major Economies - Ratopati
description: Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal Advocates for Nepal as a 'Dynamic and Reliable Bridge' Between Two Major Economies  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal has stated that Nepal's traditional geopolitical identity should be changed and the country should be developed as a 'dynamic and reliable bridge' between two major economies. He said that the strategic narrative of portraying Nepal as 'a taro between two stones' for the past century should be changed and moved forward according to the needs of the 21st century.

Addressing the 'Geopolitical Conflict in the World' book launch and panel discussion organized by the German organization Friedrich Ebert Stiftung (FES) Nepal in Kathmandu, Minister Khanal said that Nepal's foreign policy should now be concrete and result-oriented in terms of economic transformation. Discussing the impact of global political events on the lives of the Nepali people, he mentioned that the instability in the Gulf region is connected to the kitchens and daily lives of Nepalis. He argued that flight disruptions, suspension of agreements, energy price hikes, and the impact on the safety of Nepali citizens have further increased the importance of multilateral peace.

Minister Khanal stated that global adverse circumstances are hindering Nepal's goal of graduating from Least Developed Country (LDC) status by 2026. While trade is considered the engine of development, he clarified that trade alone cannot replace development assistance due to non-tariff barriers and stringent regulations in major markets.

'Asia accounts for more than 60 percent of global economic growth,' he said, 'We want to transform Nepal into a bridge connecting the rapidly developing economies of our neighbors.'

Stating that although Nepal's contribution to climate change is negligible, its risks are high, he informed that 74 billion US dollars will be needed to achieve the 'net-zero' emission target by 2045. 'This is not a plea for charity,' he said, 'This is a matter of climate justice.'

He mentioned that Nepal has been drawing the world's attention to grant-based climate finance and the 1.5-degree Celsius limit, as the Himalayan ecosystem affects the lives of billions of people. Minister Khanal portrayed Nepal's inclusive social achievements, such as constitutional protection for gender minorities, contribution-based social security, and decentralized federal representation, as Nepal's modern 'soft power.' He claimed that these reforms were made based on its own values and norms, not under external pressure.

He reiterated that Nepal will adopt an independent and non-aligned foreign policy, embracing the motto 'Friendship with all, enmity with none.' Describing foreign policy as the 'outer wing' of domestic aspirations, he said that 'economic statecraft' will now be placed at the center of diplomacy, prioritizing investment, startups, and cross-border energy corridors.

Expressing concern over the power competition and the decline of international norms seen in world affairs, he pledged that Nepal will always stand in favor of the United Nations Charter, multilateralism, and international law. Citing Buddhist philosophy for the construction of truth and wisdom, he emphasized diplomatic dialogue and integrity.

काठमांडू। विदेश मंत्री शिशिर खनाल नेपालक पारम्परिक भूराजनीतिक पहिचान मे परिवर्तन करबाक चाही आ देश केँ दूटा प्रमुख अर्थव्यवस्थाक बीच ‘गतिशील आ विश्वसनीय सेतु’क रूप मे विकसित करबाक बात कहलनि अछि । ओ कहलनि जे, विगत शताब्दी सँ नेपाल केँ ‘दू पाथरक बीच तारो’ केर रूप मे चित्रित करबाक सामरिक कथ्य केँ बदलि 21म शताब्दीक आवश्यकतानुसार आगू बढबाक चाही।

जर्मन संस्था फ्रेडरिक एबर्ट स्टिफतुंग (एफईएस) नेपाल द्वारा काठमांडू मे आयोजित ‘विश्व मे भूराजनीतिक संघर्ष’ पुस्तक विमोचन आ पैनल चर्चा केँ संबोधित करैत मंत्री खनाल आर्थिक परिवर्तनक दृष्टि सँ नेपालक विदेश नीति आब ठोस आ परिणामोन्मुख हेबाक चाही। नेपाली जनता के जीवन पर वैश्विक राजनीतिक घटना के प्रभाव के चर्चा करैत ओ खाड़ी क्षेत्र के अस्थिरता नेपाली के भनसा घर आ दैनिक जीवन स जुड़ल रहल उल्लेख केलथि । हुनकऽ तर्क छेलै कि उड़ान म॑ बाधा, समझौता निलंबन, ऊर्जा केरऽ दाम बढ़ना, आरू नेपाली नागरिकऽ के सुरक्षा प॑ पड़ै वाला प्रभाव स॑ बहुपक्षीय शांति के महत्व आरू बढ़ी गेलऽ छै ।

मंत्री खनाल नेपाल के 2026 तक अल्पविकसित देश (एलडीसी) के दर्जा स स्नातक करय के लक्ष्य मे बाधा पहुंचा रहल बतौलनि।जखन कि व्यापार के विकास के इंजन मानल जाइत अछि, ओतहि ओ स्पष्ट केलनि जे गैर-शुल्क बाधा आ प्रमुख बाजार मे कड़ा नियम के कारण विकास सहायता के जगह असगर व्यापार नहि ल सकैत अछि।

ओ कहलनि जे, वैश्विक आर्थिक विकास के 60 प्रतिशत सं बेसी एशिया के हिस्सा अछि, हम नेपाल के अपन पड़ोसी देश के तेजी सं विकसित अर्थव्यवस्था के जोड़य वाला पुल मे बदलय चाहैत छी।

जलवायु परिवर्तन में नेपाल के योगदान भले नगण्य छै, लेकिन एकरऽ जोखिम अधिक छै, ई कहतें हुअ॑ हुनी २०४५ तलक ‘नेट-जीरो’ उत्सर्जन के लक्ष्य प्राप्त करै लेली ७४ अरब अमेरिकी डॉलर के जरूरत पड़तै ।

ओ उल्लेख केलनि जे नेपाल अनुदान आधारित जलवायु वित्त आ डेढ़ डिग्री सेल्सियस सीमा दिस विश्वक ध्यान आकर्षित करैत आबि रहल अछि, कारण हिमालयी पारिस्थितिकी तंत्र अरबों लोकक जीवन प्रभावित करैत अछि । मंत्री खनाल नेपाल केरऽ समावेशी सामाजिक उपलब्धि, जेना कि लैंगिक अल्पसंख्यक केरऽ संवैधानिक संरक्षण, योगदान आधारित सामाजिक सुरक्षा, आरू विकेंद्रीकृत संघीय प्रतिनिधित्व क॑ नेपाल केरऽ आधुनिक ‘सॉफ्ट पावर’ के रूप म॑ चित्रित करलकै । हुनकऽ दावा छेलै कि ई सुधार बाहरी दबाव के तहत नै, बल्कि ओकरऽ अपनऽ मूल्य आरू मानदंड के आधार प॑ करलऽ गेलऽ छै ।

ओ दोहरौलनि जे नेपाल ‘सबक संग मित्रता, ककरो संग दुश्मनी’क आदर्श वाक्य केँ अपनाबैत स्वतंत्र आ असंरेखित विदेश नीति अपनाओत। विदेश नीति क॑ घरेलू आकांक्षा केरऽ ‘बाहरी विंग’ बताबैत॑ हुअ॑ हुनी कहलकै कि अब॑ ‘आर्थिक राज्यकला’ क॑ कूटनीति के केंद्र म॑ रखलऽ जैतै, जेकरा म॑ निवेश, स्टार्टअप, आरू सीमा पार स॑ ऊर्जा गलियारा क॑ प्राथमिकता देलऽ जैतै ।

सत्ता प्रतिस्पर्धा आरू विश्व मामला म॑ देखलऽ जाय वाला अंतर्राष्ट्रीय मानदंडऽ के पतन प॑ चिंता व्यक्त करतें हुअ॑ हुनी प्रतिज्ञा करलकै कि नेपाल हमेशा संयुक्त राष्ट्र केरऽ चार्टर, बहुपक्षीयता, आरू अंतर्राष्ट्रीय कानून के पक्ष म॑ खड़ा रहतै । सत्य आ बुद्धि के निर्माण के लेल बौद्ध दर्शन के हवाला दैत ओ कूटनीतिक संवाद आ अखंडता पर जोर देलनि ।

title: Nepal Faces Demographic Crossroads: Youth Dividend and Aging Challenges - Ratopati
description: Nepal Faces Demographic Crossroads: Youth Dividend and Aging Challenges  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. Nepal currently stands at a decisive juncture in its demographic history. The country still has a large active youth population, which can be utilized as a significant opportunity for economic development. However, at the same time, the birth rate has fallen below the replacement level, a large portion of the youth workforce is migrating abroad for employment and study, the population in rural and hilly areas is declining, and the proportion of the elderly population is rapidly increasing. In other words, Nepal is simultaneously facing the opportunity of a demographic dividend and the challenge of demographic aging.

UNFPA Nepal Representative Shreeram Hari Das has stated that Nepal's changing demographic situation should be understood not as a crisis but as an important signal for the future. According to him, viewing population change merely as an increase or decrease in the number of people can overlook the underlying social, economic, and human factors. "Demographic change is not just about a change in population numbers. It is about people, their hopes, aspirations, and the choices they can make," Hari Das said.

According to him, Nepal is currently within the window of demographic dividend as a country with a large youth population. However, this opportunity does not automatically translate into economic prosperity. If quality education, health, skills, and employment are not provided to the youth, there is a risk that a large youth population could become a source of unemployment, frustration, migration, and social dissatisfaction rather than a force for development.

The National Statistics Office's report 'Demographic Dividend in Nepal,' prepared based on the National Census 2078, also portrays Nepal's demographic situation as a transition. In 2078 BS, the median age of Nepal's population reached 26 years, up from 22 years in 2068 BS. This shows a significant upward shift in Nepal's age structure over the past decade. The same report indicates that Nepal is still in the demographic dividend phase but emphasizes the need to link this opportunity with productive economic activities. Nepal will reap demographic benefits until 2108 BS and then fully enter an aging society.

A Large Population is Not Just an Opportunity

A large youth population in Nepal has long been presented as a potential for development. Having a large working-age population is a significant economic opportunity for any country. As the proportion of working-age people increases, there is potential for increased production, consumption, savings, investment, and tax revenue. As the proportion of dependent children in families decreases, it also creates opportunities for families and the state to invest financial resources in other areas.

However, it is a mistake to understand the demographic dividend solely as a result of age structure. If a large youth population cannot be integrated with the economy, it creates pressure rather than a dividend. If the youth are educated but cannot find employment, are skilled but cannot find a market, want to be entrepreneurs but cannot find capital and markets, the demographic opportunity may be lost.

The analysis of the 2078 census by the National Statistics Office shows that the literacy rate of the population above five years has reached 76.2 percent. There has also been an improvement in labor force participation. However, the relationship between education and the labor market, the alignment of skills with the market, and productive employment for youth remain significant questions. Therefore, Nepal's current question is not just "How many young people do we have?" The real question is "Where are we utilizing the potential of those young people?"

If industries, agricultural modernization, tourism, hydropower, information technology, digital services, green economy, and entrepreneurship are not expanded within the country during the period of a large youth population, that demographic opportunity will gradually diminish. Once the youth age and the population grows older, that opportunity cannot be regained.

Youth Population and Emigration Countries

Nepal's demographic transition cannot be viewed separately from foreign migration. Millions of Nepali youth have migrated abroad in search of employment, education, and opportunities. While this has made a significant contribution to the country's economy through remittances, it has also had a profound impact on the domestic labor force, family structure, and rural population.

The analysis of youth from the National Census 2078 also shows a large proportion of absence from the country within the youth age group. Youth aged 20-24 residing abroad are primarily concentrated in the Middle East and other Asian countries. This indicates a situation where a large productive segment of Nepal's youth population, although present on paper within the country, is actually outside the country.

On the other hand, migration is often perceived as a negative event, but this is not entirely accurate. Remittances from abroad have contributed to family income, education, health, and consumption. Skills, experience, international networks, and investment can also come from abroad. This should also be viewed from the perspective of opportunity.

Therefore, the question raised by UNFPA Nepal Chief Hari Das is important. "The question is not just how to stop people from going abroad, but how to make migration a choice rather than a compulsion."

For Nepal, this means not restricting the right to go abroad, but creating opportunities within the country and ensuring an environment for safe, dignified, and productive migration for those who go abroad. It is equally important to integrate the skills and capital of returning workers into the economy.

Birth Rate Has Decreased, But This Does Not Mean Youth Do Not Want Children

The biggest change in Nepal's demographic future is the decline in the fertility rate. According to the National Census 2078, Nepal's total fertility rate has reached 1.9 per woman, which is below the replacement level of 2.1. A decline in fertility rate from over 6 in the 1970s to below 2 in four decades is a profound demographic change in Nepal.

This should not be understood with the simple conclusion that "Nepalis have stopped having children." Many factors influence fertility decisions, such as increasing age at marriage, rising female education, increasing aspirations for employment and careers, couples living separately due to foreign employment, rising costs of raising children, housing problems, employment uncertainty, and the challenge of balancing family and work.

UNFPA's latest demographic future survey has highlighted this issue globally. The study, which surveyed the views of 109,000 young people from 73 countries, shows that young people are not detached from relationships, family, and the desire for children, but economic uncertainty, employment, housing, and other structural barriers make it difficult to fulfill their aspirations.

Therefore, simply urging women to have more children because the fertility rate has decreased is not a solution. The real question is why young people are unable to have the families they desire.

As UNFPA Nepal Chief Hari Das puts it, "We should not view demographic change merely as a number of people. We must also connect it with people's hopes, aspirations, and the choices they can make."

This means that policies supporting family formation are necessary. Without policies that ensure secure employment, adequate income, housing, maternity and paternity leave, childcare services, quality health and education, and reduce the compulsion for women to choose between career and family, simply urging an increase in birth rate will not be effective.

On the Other Side of Demographic Change is an Aging Society

Another significant change in Nepal's population structure is the rapid increase in the elderly population. By 2078 BS, the population aged 65 and above has reached approximately 7 percent of the total population. Internationally, a society is considered to have entered the aging phase when the population aged 65 and above reaches 7 percent. This change is even more significant for Nepal because the country is beginning to face the challenges of an aging society before achieving full economic development.

According to the demographic analysis of the National Statistics Office, the median age of Nepal's population has increased from 22 years in 2068 BS to 26 years in 2078 BS. This indicates that the population's age structure is rapidly shifting upwards. This is a sign of an increasing elderly population.

There are three main reasons behind this change. First, the long-term decline in the fertility rate. Second, improvements in health and life expectancy. Third, the migration of the young workforce abroad and towards cities within the country.

There are no young people in the villages, but there are elderly parents. There are young people in the cities, but they are also looking for opportunities to go abroad in the future. This is changing Nepal's family structure itself.

When Villages Empty, Not Just the Population, But the State Structure Also Changes

The most serious impact of migration is seen in the geographical distribution of the population. The population in many settlements in the hilly and mountainous regions is declining, while the population is concentrating in the Terai and large cities. This affects everything from electoral constituencies to schools, health facilities, local government resource allocation, and infrastructure utilization. In villages with declining populations, schools become studentless, health facilities are underutilized, and local markets shrink. Ultimately, the returns on public infrastructure may also weaken.

Therefore, efforts to stop migration alone are not enough. An environment must be created where people want to stay in the villages. Rural population rebalancing is possible only by integrating employment, education, health, digital access, agricultural markets, tourism, small industries, and local entrepreneurship.

Nepal's demographic map is no longer just a story of increasing population in Kathmandu, Pokhara, Biratnagar, or Terai cities. It is a question of where people will live, where they will work, where they will form families, and where the state will have to provide services in the future.

Economic Value of an Aging Society

As the elderly population increases, not only social security expenses rise, but it also impacts the labor market, tax system, health services, family structure, and public expenditure. As the working-age population declines, the economy will have to produce more with less manpower. This means that significant investment in technology, skills, and human capital will be necessary to increase productivity.

The impact on the health sector is even more evident. As the risk of chronic diseases increases with age, the demand for hospitals, medicines, health insurance, home-based care, and long-term care services will rise.

However, it is also a mistake to view the elderly population solely as an expense. Elderly citizens possess experience, skills, social knowledge, and locally accumulated knowledge over generations. Their role can be redefined in agriculture, handicrafts, culture, education, community leadership, and skill transfer. Future elderly policy should not just be about distributing old-age pensions; it should be a policy for building healthy, active, and dignified aging.

Has the Government's Policy and Budget Read the Demographic Signals?

It is at this point that Nepal's policy and programs and the budget for the fiscal year 2081/82 (Note: Although 2083/84 is mentioned in the original article, the year can be adjusted to be relevant to the current time, however, here it is kept as 2083/84 as per the source) should be viewed from a demographic perspective. The government has presented a budget of Rs 21 kharba 24 arab 34 crore for the fiscal year 2083/84.

The budget prioritizes programs related to employment, skill development, entrepreneurship, production, and the labor market. Only Rs 3.63 arba has been allocated to the labor and employment sector, which includes programs for safe foreign employment, skill development, welfare of migrant workers, and channeling remittances into productive sectors.

This is an important aspect connected to Nepal's demographic situation. This is because a large segment of Nepal's youth population is already entering the labor market. If opportunities are not provided within the country, a significant portion of the demographic dividend will be produced abroad.

However, when viewed from a broader demographic perspective, questions remain. Are programs to provide employment to youth integrated with policies necessary for family formation, such as housing, childcare, maternity and paternity security, and reproductive health? Is the healthcare needs of the aging population, created by the out-migration of youth from villages, adequately addressed as a long-term priority in the budget? Is the economy for long-term care being prepared for Nepal, which is on the verge of entering an aging society?

The answers to these questions cannot be found by simply looking for "youth programs" or "old-age pensions" in the budget. A demographic budget is not a budget that allocates money based on age groups; it is a budget that invests by anticipating the changes that the population structure will bring to the economy, families, labor market, and public services.

In this sense, although the budget shows positive foundations in terms of youth, skills, and employment, the form of a clear "demographic budget" that binds Nepal's overall demographic transition into a single strategic framework still needs to be developed. The Government of Nepal has already started implementing the budget, so now the budget should be evaluated not only by the size of its expenditure but also by how well its priorities align with Nepal's changing age structure, migration patterns, and fertility behavior.

Youth Policy Must Also Be Part of Demographic Strategy

Nepal has legally and policy-wise defined youth differently. The National Youth Council Act, 2072, defines youth as those aged 16 to 40. However, the new National Youth Policy, 2082, limits the youth age group to 18 to 35 years.

This change should not be seen merely as an administrative redefinition of age. It is linked to how the state understands youth. Today's youth generation is more educated, digitally connected, aware of global opportunities, and desires more choices regarding their personal lives than the previous generation.

The analysis of youth by the National Statistics Office also shows that youth's education, marriage, fertility, migration, and employment cannot be understood as separate issues. For example, in 2078 BS, 21.9 percent of women aged 20-24 had already married before the age of 18. At the same time, the adolescent fertility rate has significantly decreased compared to previous decades.

This means that there are two different demographic realities in Nepal at the same time. In some communities, child marriage and early motherhood are still issues, while on the other hand, among urban, educated, and economically active youth, the age of marriage and childbirth is being postponed.

Therefore, a single national policy is not sufficient for everyone. Nepal's demographic policy should address the different realities according to region, province, class, gender, education, and economic status.

Understand "Fertility Choice" Before "Fertility Crisis"

Globally, the debate on fertility rates is intense. A few decades ago, the main concern was overpopulation. Today, declining birth rates and aging populations have become major concerns in many countries, including China, the UK, South Korea, Japan, and Italy.

UNFPA has advanced this debate in a new way through its report 'The Real Fertility Crisis: Exploring Fertility Rights and Self-Determination in a Changing World.' The report urges that low birth rates should not be seen as a simple consequence of people not wanting children, but rather linked to structural barriers that prevent people from forming the families they desire. UNFPA's Asia-Pacific regional report also notes this shift towards viewing it from the perspective of fertility decisions and reproductive security.

This perspective is also useful in Nepal. If young couples want two children but do not have stable employment, do not have a house, lack childcare arrangements, and one partner is forced to work abroad, then having fewer children is more of a compulsion than their personal "unwillingness." Therefore, Nepal's demographic policy should move beyond "have more children" or "have fewer children" policies and focus on the question of "How to create an environment where people can form the families they desire?"

Why is Demographic Intelligence Necessary?

The concept that connects all these discussions is Demographic Intelligence. Demographic intelligence is not just about census or population data collection. It involves understanding, based on facts and analysis, where the population is growing, where it is declining, which age groups are increasing, which are decreasing, why people are migrating, why marriage is being delayed, why the number of children is decreasing, where youth are seeking employment, where the elderly are concentrating, and what impact these changes have on education, health, labor, economy, politics, and social security.

Nepal's census is providing the necessary data. The National Statistics Office has recently begun presenting demographic facts analytically through thematic reports such as 'Demographic Dividend in Nepal' and 'Adolescents and Youth in Nepal.' The need now is to link that data with the policy-making and decision-making systems of ministries, provinces, and local governments.

Where to add schools? Where to merge schools? Where are hospitals needed? Where will elderly care centers be required? In which areas should youth entrepreneurship be prioritized? In which local units is the population declining? In which places is housing policy needed? In which provinces should health and reproductive services be expanded? The answers to these questions should be sought not from political speculation, but from demographic facts and forecasts.

What is the Signal of Nepal's Future?

The biggest paradox of Nepal's demographic future is this: the country has a great opportunity with a large youth population today, but this same generation is migrating abroad; the birth rate is declining, yet many young people say they cannot form the families they desire; the elderly population is increasing, but the infrastructure needed for an aging society is insufficient; the population is declining in villages, but the pressure of population management is increasing in cities. Therefore, the next decade is crucial for Nepal.

If today's youth population can be connected with education, skills, health, employment, entrepreneurship, and production, Nepal can make the demographic dividend the basis for economic transformation. However, if the youth generation cannot be given opportunities, they will migrate abroad, villages will empty, family structures will change, and in a few decades, Nepal will have a large elderly population, but perhaps without a sufficient economic base to support it. Therefore, Nepal's demographic future is not about increasing or decreasing the population.

What kind of population structure should be created, how to make it productive, and how to build a socio-economic environment where people can form the lives and families they desire? This is the crucial question today.

As UNFPA Nepal Chief Hari Das said, "Our responsibility is to provide every young person with opportunities, information, and the necessary support so that they can transform their aspirations into reality and contribute to the nation's future."

Nepal's future development policy, therefore, is at a stage where it needs to shift from population counting to human capital strategy. Youth policy, labor policy, education policy, health policy, foreign employment policy, social security policy, housing policy, and economic policy need to be integrated under a single demographic future strategy, rather than as separate programs. This is because Nepal's demographic opportunity will not remain open forever.

Today's youth population is tomorrow's elderly population. If they are not given opportunities today, the economic base to support tomorrow's aging society will be weakened. If an environment conducive to family formation is not created today, tomorrow's population structure will change accordingly. And if migration is not managed today, the geographical population structure of Nepal tomorrow may be completely different from today.

Therefore, the main need for Nepal's demographic future is not an campaign for population control or population growth. The need is to read the demographic facts in time, identify future signals from them, and build the capacity to change the state's policies, budgets, and development priorities accordingly. In this sense, Nepal is not just in demographic transition; Nepal is at a juncture of demographic decision-making.
